Securitize to Acquire River One, Expanding Into $6 Trillion Asset-Backed Finance Market

Tokenization platform Securitize (NYSE: $SECZ) agreed Monday to acquire River One, an institutional asset-backed financing platform built around the stablecoin economy, as it expands into a private asset-backed finance market estimated at more than $6 trillion.

The acquisition, announced alongside Securitize's third-quarter financial results, would expand its tokenization infrastructure into warehouse financing, allowing institutions to borrow against pools of loans and other assets before selling, refinancing or otherwise distributing them. The deal also represents the first major deployment of the roughly $400 million CEO Carlos Domingo told said in July the company planned to allocate toward acquisitions following its public listing.

According to Securitize's earnings announcement, River One was incubated by Framework Ventures and backed by Framework and Maple Finance. The transaction is expected to close in the fourth quarter, subject to customary closing conditions. Financial terms were not disclosed.

Domingo described credit as "one of the most exciting emerging asset classes" for blockchain-based financial markets. The private asset-backed finance market was valued at approximately $6.1 trillion in 2024 and is projected to exceed $9 trillion by 2029, according to a KKR report cited by CoinDesk.

Securitize also reported third-quarter revenue of $18.6 million, up 13% from $16.5 million a year earlier and 29% from the second quarter. Tokenization revenue climbed 28% to $11.5 million, while asset servicing revenue declined 6% to $7.2 million. Average tokenized assets on the platform reached a record $5.0 billion, an increase of 39%, with $4.8 billion in assets on the platform as of Sept. 30. Transaction volume increased 20% to $4.3 billion. Meanwhile, assets under administration in its fund services business fell 29% to $25.2 billion.

The company reported a net loss of $66.3 million, or $0.41 per diluted share, compared with net income of $4.1 million in the same quarter last year. Approximately $60 million, or roughly 90% of the reported loss, stemmed from largely non-cash expenses and accounting charges associated with its business combination and public listing. These included a $23.2 million change in the fair value of earnout liabilities and a $20.6 million loss related to the settlement of convertible instruments.

This article first appeared on GuruFocus.

Amazon.com (NASDAQ:AMZN) shares advanced 4.05% to $269.79 as of 10:44 a.m. ET on Monday, November 9, in regular trading, after JPMorgan's Doug Anmuth named the company a top AI pick on the bank's focus list. Anmuth wrote that Amazon "now expects AWS revenue growth of 40%+ in 2027 & 2028," with AWS reaching $1 trillion in revenue within five to ten years and "improving capex payback."

Warning! GuruFocus has detected 5 Warning Signs with AMZN.

AMZN GF Value chart

The evidence sits in Amazon's own numbers. The company said AWS grew 39.3% in the third quarter, its sixth straight quarter of acceleration and fastest pace in nearly five years. Backlog reached $578 billion, up triple digits year over year. CEO Andy Jassy said Amazon is installing an AI accelerator about every 14 seconds. Revenue commitments for its Graviton and Trainium chips each rose more than 20x, and Bedrock token volume climbed roughly 17x.

Amazon scores 94/100 on GuruFocus's GF Score, powered by a 10/10 Growth rank, 8/10 Profitability and 8/10 Momentum. Financial Strength is the softest dimension at 7/10, a fair reading for a company pouring cash into AI capacity, and GF Value Rank sits at 7/10 with the price about 4% above the GF Value of $258.50. Simple math shows the stakes of JPMorgan's call: growth of 40% for two straight years nearly doubles a revenue base, since 1.4 times 1.4 equals 1.96. The risk is cost, not demand, because capex payback decides whether that growth lifts free cash flow or absorbs it. The next checkpoint is fourth-quarter AWS growth holding near 40% alongside steady AWS margins.

title: Amazon Is “the Cheapest It’s Been” in Years. Its P/E Fell From 34 to 21
detail:
Amazon Is “the Cheapest It’s Been” in Years. Its P/E Fell From 34 to 21
Gian Estrada
Mon, November 9, 2026 at 11:32 AM CST 4 min read
AMZN
Trade AMZN on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Amazon Is "the Cheapest It's Been" in Years. Its P/E Fell From 34 to 21 ©Syammasfitria Studio and Tiger Lily from Pexels via Canva
Key Takeaways

Amazon's P/E has fallen from 34 to 21 over the past year, and its forward P/E of 25x sits near a five-year low.

AWS grew 39% last quarter, and analysts expect normalized EPS to nearly double by 2028.

The risk is cash: free cash flow was a $34.8 billion outflow in the third quarter, and analysts expect it to stay negative through 2027.

The Nov. 5 tech sell-off hit anything tied to data centers, and few companies are building more of them than Amazon (AMZN:NASDAQ).

One panelist on CNBC's Halftime Report said the selling overshot: "Amazon is at the cheapest it's been, frankly, in years and years and years."

He has a point. Amazon's P/E has fallen from 34 to 21 over the past year, according to Creative Planning's Charlie Bilello, even as AWS grows at what CEO Andy Jassy called "our fastest growth in nearly five years."

Priced for the Spending

Bilello summed up what changed in a separate post: "Big tech is undergoing a fundamental transformation, shifting from asset-light to asset-heavy business models."

Amazon still expects about $220 billion of cash capital spending this year, up from $128.3 billion in 2025, and spent $75.9 billion in the third quarter, net of sale proceeds and incentives. Most of it goes to AWS, which took 76% of the property and equipment Amazon added in the first half of 2026. The stock has been marked down as the bill has grown.

The Growth Is Still There

AWS revenue grew 39% in the third quarter to $46.0 billion, an annual run rate of about $184 billion. Jassy expects AWS to grow more than 40% in both 2027 and 2028, and its backlog reached $578 billion, more than three years of revenue at today's pace.

Analysts expect that growth to reach earnings, with normalized EPS nearly doubling from $7.17 in 2025 to $13.99 in 2028.

AMZN Normalized EPS, Actual and Consensus Estimates: 2023-2028 (TIKR)

Reported earnings flatter Amazon this year: they include $62.8 billion of pre-tax gains on its Anthropic stake in the first half alone. On the normalized earnings analysts expect over the next 12 months, Amazon trades at 25x.

AMZN Stock NTM P/E: 2021-2026 (TIKR)

That's close to the five-year low of 23x it hit on Oct. 30, and about half its five-year average of 48x.

title: AI Agents Are “an Existential Risk to DoorDash”? Seriously? I’ll Take the Under
detail:
AI Agents Are “an Existential Risk to DoorDash”? Seriously? I’ll Take the Under
Michael Douglass
Mon, November 9, 2026 at 12:43 PM CST 4 min read
DASH
AMZN
UBER
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
AI Agents Are "an Existential Risk to DoorDash"? Seriously? I'll Take the Under ©@Prostock-Studio from Getty Images via Canva, @ckstockphoto via Canva
Key Takeaways

Last week Jason Lemkin called AI agents an existential risk to DoorDash.

I think that's crap, for a number of reasons. Starting with the fact that an agent still needs a delivery network, and DoorDash has the biggest one, plus over 35 million members who already pay it for free delivery.

AI agents have placed only several hundred DoorDash orders, against 993 million orders last quarter, and analysts expect DoorDash's revenue to nearly double from 2025 to 2028.

DoorDash traded at 28x forward earnings before Thursday's drop, well below its three-year average of 39x.

DoorDash (DASH:NASDAQ) has had a rough couple of weeks.

Shares sank 13% last Thursday after Amazon (AMZN:NASDAQ) made Uber Eats its restaurant delivery partner for Prime. Members now get free delivery on Uber Eats orders of $25 or more, placed right on Amazon. That puts Uber (UBER:NYSE), DoorDash's main rival, in front of Prime members across the U.S.

It also adds to a fear that's been hanging over the stock: that AI agents will cut DoorDash out of ordering altogether. Even so, CEO Tony Xu said on DoorDash's third-quarter call that agents had placed "several hundred orders in total" so far. DoorDash handled 993 million orders in that quarter alone.

That figure came up on this week's episode of the 20VC podcast. SaaStr founder Jason Lemkin's take?

"Agents are an existential risk to DoorDash because their number three competitor is nobody."

Which…what?

TIKR tracks 42 analysts on DoorDash. How many say "Buy"?

Several hundred orders, for now

I take his point to be this: once an agent orders your dinner, it checks DoorDash and Uber Eats and picks the cheaper one. With no third app in the race, whoever owns the agent owns the customer.

And sure, it's early. Nobody knows how many dinners agents will be ordering five years from now.

But Wall Street isn't expecting customers to flee. Analysts expect DoorDash's revenue to climb from $13.7 billion in 2025 to $25.7 billion in 2028:

DoorDash (DASH): revenue, actual and consensus estimates, $ billions, fiscal 2023-2028 (TIKR)

Prime members have had a free Grubhub+ perk since 2022, and DoorDash kept growing the whole time. I don't expect the switch to Uber Eats to move things much. And also…

The membership picks the app

Even in Lemkin's world, an agent can't drive a burrito across town. It has to hand the order to a delivery network, and DoorDash runs the biggest one. It took 59% of delivery-app spending in the third quarter, according to Consumer Edge card data. Uber Eats and Instacart each took 18%.
